\section[\hi{शुभ} \hi{दोपहर}]{\hi{शुभ} \hi{दोपहर} (shubh dopahar) — "good afternoon," this arc's rarest greeting}

\label{lesson:HI-C33-shubh-dopahar}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} You already know \hi{दोपहर}'s meaning widened from "precisely noon" to "the afternoon." This greeting rides that widened sense — but it's the least commonly heard of the three you've now met.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \hi{शुभ} \hi{दोपहर} — "good afternoon," using the widened \hi{स}ense}
\textbf{\hi{शुभ} \hi{दोपहर}} (\textbf{shubh dopahar}) — "\textbf{good afternoon}" — pairs \textbf{\hi{शुभ}} ("good") with \textbf{\hi{दोपहर}} used in the \textbf{widened, modern sense} from last lesson: "the afternoon" generally, not the narrow etymological "exactly noon." Good news for consistency: this greeting confirms \hi{दोपहर}'s widened meaning is the one people actually reach for here — nobody uses \hi{शुभ} \hi{दोपहर} to mean "good {[}precise instant of{]} noon."

\subsection*{You'll want to know — Be honest: the rarest of the three, not just another formal phrase}
Here's the twist this lesson adds, verified independently rather than assumed from \hi{सुप्रभात} or \hi{शुभ} \hi{संध्या}'s pattern: of this arc's three \hi{शुभ}+timeword greetings, \textbf{\hi{शुभ} \hi{दोपहर} is described as the rarest} in actual spoken use — even more so than the other two. Sources call it formal/written, note that casual alternatives like \textbf{\hi{आपका} \hi{दोपहर} \hi{शुभ} \hi{हो}} ("may your afternoon be good") exist but are themselves still uncommon, and confirm \textbf{\hi{नमस्ते}}/\textbf{\hi{नमस्कार}} do the real everyday greeting work across the whole afternoon, same as for morning and evening. This isn't just "another formal Sanskrit-style greeting" — it's the weakest-attested of the three, a genuine difference in \textbf{degree}, not just the same story repeated a third time.

  \item {[}YOU SAY: \hi{नमस्ते}/\hi{नमस्कार} — the real everyday greeting, covering afternoons too{]}
